column4: The verse says these people come to prayer lazily and spend only reluctantly; it makes expenditure itself a test of sincerity, beyond the section's boast of having spent much.
Some Bedouins treat what they spend as a loss or penalty and await misfortune for the believers; this is a direct contrary account of spending to the section's boastful claim.
Other Bedouins treat their spending as a means of closeness to God and the Messenger; the verse gives the opposite purpose from counting expenditure for public reputation.

The verse distinguishes wealth given to increase among people's possessions from charity given seeking God's face, which is multiplied; this directly separates public advantage from divine accounting.
These believers spend from what God provided secretly and openly, seeking a trade that will not fail; it answers the section's depleted tally with expenditure whose return is secured with God.
The next ayah says God will give them their full reward and increase them from His bounty; it completes 35:29's image of a trade that does not perish.
The source section's lisan and shafah dictionary glosses concern praise among people; this says honor belongs to God, and that good words and righteous deeds rise to Him.

The people say they did not hide themselves expecting their hearing, sight, and skins to testify against them, but thought God did not know much of their deeds; this directly reverses the section's assumption that no one saw.
This person withholds and considers himself self-sufficient, a close parallel to the section's false self-assessment and a reversal of its boast about consuming wealth.
He also denies the best; the verse identifies the belief that accompanies his withholding, rather than treating his wealth as an achievement.
God eases him toward hardship; this continues the reversal of the self-sufficient person's estimate of what his wealth secures.
When he falls, his wealth does not benefit him; this directly counters the section's speaker treating the use or loss of money as a boast.
The command not to oppress the orphan reverses the treatment of vulnerable people against which the section sets its giving.
The command not to repel the asker connects to the section's ش ف ه dictionary sense of requests exhausting a holder, but directs the holder to respond without rejection.
The section's قول and lisan discussion concerns public mention; this commands the hearer to speak of the Lord's favor, making remembrance of the giver the ground of speech rather than self-praise.
The hypocrites show their prayer to people and remember God little; this is another Qur'anic formulation of the section's root رءي as public performance.
The day comes when mouths are sealed and hands speak while feet testify; the speaker's own body answers the section's boastful spoken claim and assumption of no witness.
The verse says that if people possessed the treasuries of their Lord's mercy they would still withhold for fear of spending; this names the opposite calculation to a boast about consuming wealth.
People are called to spend in God's way, and the verse says some are miserly and that the one who withholds only withholds from himself; this reverses the section's boastful accounting of wealth.
Believers are told to spend from what God has made them successors over; the verse makes possession entrusted by God, against the speaker's self-crediting total.
The Ansar prefer others over themselves even when in need; this gives a concrete form of giving whose motive is another person's benefit, not applause.
The command says to spend for your own good and praises those protected from their own stinginess; this directly contrasts giving with hoarding or self-serving display.
The surah opens with a warning to those who give short measure; it brings the section's concern with counting wealth into a concrete scene of dishonest measurement.
They take full measure when measuring for themselves; this exposes the self-favoring calculation behind treating one's own total as the only relevant account.
They give others less when measuring or weighing for them; this reverses the speaker's self-presentation by judging the amount from the recipient's side.
Those who withhold what God has given are warned that it will be placed around their necks; this counters treating retained wealth as a safe measure of one's standing.

The verse lists accumulated gold and silver, horses, livestock, and crops among worldly attractions; it supplies concrete forms of wealth behind the section's account of مال and its older livestock sense.
The source section's dictionary gloss says Arab wealth was often livestock; this verse names cattle among the provisions given to a people, showing that material wealth could be herds.
The question asks whether wealth and children are thought to be good things hastened to people; it exposes the false measure of favor that the section's self-assessing spender assumes.
The next ayah answers that such people do not perceive; it completes the correction of the assumption in 23:55 that abundant possessions prove success.
The command to give full measure and weigh with a straight balance offers a concrete standard against self-serving calculation of amounts.
Believers are told to spend from what God provided before a Day with no trade or friendship; this places expenditure within an account that public reputation cannot settle.
Satan's promise of poverty gives a specific fear behind withholding wealth; it contrasts with the section's claim that a large expenditure is only a lost sum.
These people are not distracted by trade from God's remembrance, prayer, and giving; this counters making wealth and public notice the center of one's conduct.
The command joins fair measure and balance with guarding an orphan's property; it connects the section's account of quantities to the vulnerable person whose due can be lost.
The verse warns not to be impressed by the hypocrites' wealth and children; it addresses the audience response that a public material display seeks.
This repeats the warning not to be impressed by their wealth and children; its recurrence underlines that visible abundance is not evidence of divine favor.
This follows the catalogue of worldly attractions in 3:14 with what is better with God; it supplies the measure beyond the wealth and livestock just listed.

The source section uses لُبَدًا for wealth in heaps; this ayah uses a related form for a crowd pressing around the servant. The sense differs, so this is a weak possible echo: abundance and a public audience meet in the section, though the crowd here belongs to a different scene.
